cues.zh: 大家好，我是

Thank you for being here. This talk is called,
cues.zh: 我是 Peter Alvaro，加州大学圣克鲁兹分校的计算机科学助理教授。很高兴能来到这里。早上的主题演讲时段通常是补觉的好时间，说实话我睡过很多次，次数多得我都不好意思承认。所以感谢大家没有这么做，感谢你们来到这里。这次演讲的题目是，

And it's really the backstory of a tiny little boutique language called Daedalus that my colleagues at UC Berkeley and I developed during my first couple years at Berkeley and which sort of formed the rock on which I built all of my thesis work and hopefully, with any luck, another ten years of good research. I never got to go back and tell the story of that little language,
cues.zh: 我明白你的意思。一门微小的语言能让我们学到关于庞大系统的什么。这其实是关于一门叫 Daedalus 的小众小语言背后的故事，它是我和我在 UC Berkeley 的同事在我到 Berkeley 的头几年开发的，某种程度上构成了基石，我所有论文工作都建立在它之上，希望运气好的话，还能支撑未来十年好的研究。我一直没能回过头去讲那门小语言的故事，

cues.en: the context out of which it arose,
cues.zh: 它诞生的背景，

cues.en: some of the design decisions we made. So I wanna thank you for being my captive audience in this somewhat historical narrative and expect,
cues.zh: 我们当时做的一些设计决策。所以我要感谢大家在这段略显历史回顾的叙述中充当我的忠实听众，并且期待，

cues.zh: 我发现，对于这类受邀演讲，一个很好的开场方式就是先抛出一些非常有力的观点，你懂的，就是那些发自内心的观点

cues.en: Abstraction is sometimes harmful.
cues.zh: 抽象有时是有害的。

cues.en: So abstraction is a thing. It's arguably the the the best tool that we have in computer science and in cognition generally for managing complexity
cues.zh: 抽象是个好东西，可以说是我们计算机科学乃至整个认知领域中应对复杂性的最佳工具。

cues.en: and for moving beyond it. And at least in computer science, it works like this. We labor
cues.zh: 并以此实现超越。至少在计算机科学领域，它是这样运作的。我们付出努力

cues.en: at something
cues.zh: 在某件事上

cues.en: with computers and we build an object of significant
cues.zh: 用计算机，我们构建一个意义重大的对象

cues.en: complexity and perhaps even profound beauty. And then, you know, we finish laboring on it and it comes time to think about the ways in which it will be used
cues.zh: 复杂性，或许还有深刻的美感。然后，你知道，当我们辛苦完成它之后，就该考虑它会被如何使用。

cues.en: and reused.
cues.zh: 并被重复使用。

cues.en: So we ask, we draw a line of demarcation over that object and we ask ourselves, what are the details
cues.zh: 所以我们在那个对象上划出一条界线，然后问自己：具体细节是什么？

cues.en: that are essential?
cues.zh: 哪些是必不可少的？

cues.en: Well, what does essential mean? Well, essential to some domain that we think the object will be used in. And we obscure
cues.zh: 那么，什么叫“必不可少”？就是对于我们认为对象会被使用的某个领域来说，必不可少。我们把它隐藏了起来。

cues.en: the other details of the object. Right? We do this anytime we take a bunch of code and put it in a function and make decisions about what parameters to expose, what what to return. We do this when we group together a bunch of functions with similar... With with related functionality into a shared library.
cues.zh: 对象的其他细节，对吧？每当我们把一堆代码放进一个函数，并决定要暴露哪些参数、返回什么时，我们都会这么做。把一组功能相近……也就是相关功能的函数放进一个共享库时，我们也会这么做。

cues.en: We do this when we group together a bunch of functionality behind an API that we expose at our service boundary, but nowhere are these sorts of distinctions so stark
cues.zh: 当我们把一堆功能打包到一个 API 中、并在服务边界上对外暴露时，就会这么做，但这种区分方式在任何地方都不算特别明显。

cues.en: as when we design languages. And then of course the hope is at that interface boundary we expose those details that really matter
cues.zh: 就像我们设计语言时一样。当然，我们希望在接口边界上暴露出那些真正重要的细节。

cues.en: and then a thousand flowers will bloom. Right?
cues.zh: 然后就会百花齐放，对吧？

cues.en: You know, thousands of applications. Applications we could never even have predicted will use our interface and make progress without having to concern themselves with the the hardcore details of the implementation. Right? And that's a good thing.
cues.zh: 你知道，成千上万的应用程序。有些应用我们根本无法预料，它们会使用我们的接口并取得进展，而不必去操心那些底层实现的具体细节。对吧？这是一件好事。

cues.en: And sometimes it's even better than that because sometimes the act of hiding can illuminate
cues.zh: 有时甚至比这更好，因为有时候隐藏反而能带来启发

cues.en: surprising things. Right? If you take... If you blow away a haystack, all of a sudden there's all these shiny needles. Right? And so in this talk for example, I hope to show how by papering over a lot of the distinctions between,
cues.zh: 让人意想不到的收获。对吧？如果你……如果你把草堆吹开，突然间就会发现里面全是闪闪发光的针。对吧？比如在这次演讲中，我希望能展示如何通过抹平很多……之间的区别，

cues.en: you know, different kinds of state representation
cues.zh: 你知道，有各种不同的状态表示方式

cues.en: and different patterns for control flow and synchronization.
cues.zh: 以及用于控制流和同步的不同模式。

cues.en: Oh, that shouldn't have got... That should have gone away too. We... That's one of the things that was supposed to drop off. We can illuminate
cues.zh: 哦，那个本来不该……那个也应该消失掉。我们……那是本该被去掉的东西之一。我们可以高亮显示。

cues.en: the real matter
cues.zh: 真正的问题

cues.en: in the domain of distributed systems. Data
cues.zh: 在分布式系统领域。数据

cues.en: moving
cues.zh: 移动

cues.en: and changing
cues.zh: 并且不断变化

cues.en: through space and time.
cues.zh: 穿越时空。

cues.en: Okay?
cues.zh: 明白了。请发送需要翻译的英文字幕内容，我会按要求逐句翻译并保留分隔符。

cues.en: But it's not all good, you know. When we forget and and and we do forget that abstraction
cues.zh: 但这并不全是好事，你知道的。当我们遗忘的时候——我们确实会遗忘——那种抽象

cues.en: is a universal
cues.zh: 是一个通用的

cues.en: activity of computer users. It's something that we all do to manage our own complexities.
cues.zh: 计算机用户的一种活动。我们都会这样做，来管理自身的复杂性。

cues.en: We get lazy and we tend to think of abstractions as these fixed boundaries, you know, these walls.
cues.zh: 我们变得懒惰，倾向于把抽象当成固定的边界，你知道的，就像一堵堵墙。

cues.en: And walls are intended to create borders,
cues.zh: 而墙的目的就是划定边界，

cues.en: to prevent things from flowing across them.
cues.zh: 阻止事物穿过它们流动。

cues.en: We're still walls pen people in.
cues.zh: 我们仍然是把人圈起来的墙。

cues.en: And when you think about it, who do we put below the wall on the hard side? Well, we put us. Right? We put the geniuses,
cues.zh: 仔细想想，墙的困难一侧下面放的是谁？嗯，是我们。对吧？我们放的是那些天才，

cues.en: the infrastructure programmers, the 10 x engineers, the library writers. Okay? And then and then who goes above the wall? Well, the the despised
cues.zh: 基础设施程序员、10x 工程师、库作者。对吧？然后，然后谁翻过墙？嗯，那些被鄙视的

cues.en: users.
cues.zh: 用户。

cues.en: The the the programmers with neckties, the COBOL people, the SQL people, the analysts. We hate those guys. Read the fucking manual we say to those guys.
cues.zh: 那些打领带的程序员，搞 COBOL 的、搞 SQL 的、还有分析师们。我们讨厌那帮人。我们会对他们说：自己去看那该死的手册。

cues.en: And that's just something that's always made me really sad. This belief that like library writers and library users are two different classes of people as opposed to two different phases in a programmer's life or maybe even just the arc of an application's life or something like that. It makes me sad.
cues.zh: 而这一直让我很难过。把库的编写者和库的使用者看成两类不同的人，而不是程序员人生中的两个不同阶段，或者甚至只是应用程序生命周期中的两个阶段之类的，这种观念让我很难过。

cues.en: But it also makes me concerned
cues.zh: 但这也让我担心

cues.en: because if we respect
cues.zh: 因为如果我们尊重

cues.en: those users... By the way, those users are the people who are using computers to like do real shit, get shit done, like do science. They're the reason that we exist. Right? If we respect them so little,
cues.zh: 那些用户……顺便说一句，那些用户就是用电脑真正干实事的人，把事办成，比如搞科研。他们正是我们存在的原因。对吧？如果我们这么不尊重他们，

cues.en: what are the odds that we're providing the right interfaces for them?
cues.zh: 我们为它们提供合适接口的几率有多大？

cues.en: One more word about abstraction.
cues.zh: 关于抽象，我还想再说一句。

cues.en: There there remain certain domains, I'm thinking about one in particular, that remain stubbornly
cues.zh: 仍然存在一些领域——我脑海里就有一个特别典型的——它们始终固执地

cues.en: difficult to create the right abstractions for. Right? It would be extremely tempting to paper over the complexity of physical distribution. It would it would simplify the models we use to interact with large scale systems.
cues.zh: 难以建立起恰当的抽象。对吧？掩盖物理分布的复杂性，这种想法极其诱人。这本可以简化我们与大规模系统交互的模型。

cues.en: But unfortunately attempts to do so represent
cues.zh: 但遗憾的是，这类尝试往往构成了

cues.en: some of the worst failures of abstraction in the history of computing. I'm thinking about stuff like RPC,
cues.zh: 计算史上最惨痛的一些抽象失败案例。我指的就是像 RPC 这种东西，

cues.en: you know. I'm gonna put a function on some other computer and pretend it's online, what could go wrong?
cues.zh: 你知道的。“我要把一个函数放在另一台机器上，假装它就在本地，能出什么岔子？”

cues.en: Or you know, I'm gonna put a disk on some other computer and pretend it's in my computer, what could go wrong?
cues.zh: 或者，“我要把一块磁盘放在另一台机器上，假装它就在我的电脑里，能出什么岔子？”

cues.en: And the jury isn't out on this one yet, distributed transactions, but it does seem kind of dicey
cues.zh: 还有分布式事务，目前尚无定论，但看起来确实挺悬的——

cues.en: that you you could take a database that's literally distributed all around the world and pretend it's it's on it's on a tower under my desk and that I can do anything with it I could do with that tower under my desk. Okay? I mean, we can paper over these things and and they're gonna do more than leak.
cues.zh: 你把一个实打实分布在全球的数据库，假装成就在我桌底下的主机箱里，假装能对它为所欲为。对吧？我是说，我们可以粉饰这些问题，但结果可远不止是抽象泄漏那么简单。

cues.en: Right?
cues.zh: 对吧？

cues.en: So... Okay. Enough about enough about abstraction. Let me talk about me for a minute.
cues.zh: 所以……好吧。关于抽象就聊这么多。接下来稍微谈谈我自己。

cues.en: I'm not a big fan of about me slides, I can't really tell the story of Daedalus without telling a little bit about the story of me. And the first thing to get out of the way is that I'm not a lifelong hacker.
cues.zh: 我并不喜欢“个人简介”这种幻灯片，但不交代一点我的背景，就很难讲清楚 Daedalus 的故事。首先要说明的是，我并不是那种从小写到大的黑客。

cues.en: I'm not one of those people. I I screwed around with computers a little bit when I was a lad but I barely touched them in college apart from word processors and it wasn't till I moved to the Bay Area around the year 2000 and had to get work that I started like, you know, writing code for a living. I was working at a company that you may have heard of called Ask Jeeves, it's an early internet company
cues.zh: 我不是那类人。小时候我稍微鼓捣过电脑，但在大学里除了用字处理软件外几乎没碰过，直到 2000 年左右我搬到湾区，为了讨生活，才开始写代码维生。当时我在一家你们可能听过的公司工作，叫 Ask Jeeves，一家早期的互联网公司，

cues.en: and my team was called data engineering. We were responsible for the whole life cycle of user generated data at the site finding its way through our infrastructure in this... A SQL Server.
cues.zh: 我的团队叫数据工程。我们负责网站上用户生成数据的完整生命周期，让它们穿过我们的基础设施，最终流向……一台 SQL Server。

cues.en: So I was living in two very different modes at Ask Jeeves. I was writing a lot of like infrastructure code, distributed systems code in the language that you may have heard of called C.
cues.zh: 所以在 Ask Jeeves 时，我处于两种截然不同的工作模式。我写了大量的底层基础设施代码、分布式系统代码，用的是大家可能听说过的 C 语言。

cues.en: And then, you know, I was, you know,
cues.zh: 然后，你们懂的，我还在……

cues.en: moving
cues.zh: 搬运

cues.en: the data around, replicating it, transforming it, loading it in the database. And then once it got in the databases,
cues.zh: 数据，做复制、转换，再把它们加载进数据库。而一旦数据落库，

cues.en: I was writing a lot of
cues.zh: 我又得写大量的……

cues.en: I was writing a lot of reports on it in a language that you may have heard of called SQL,
cues.zh: 我又用大家可能听说过的 SQL 语言写了大量的报表，

cues.en: you know, business reports and and rudimentary predictive analytics stuff. So it really had two hats and switching back and forth between them. And what I... You see,
cues.zh: 比如业务报表，还有一些基础的预测分析。所以我实际上身兼两职，来回切换。而我……你们看，

cues.en: I felt like this guy.
cues.zh: 我觉得自己就像这家伙一样。

cues.en: Because what I was doing was really hard, but the thing was I was good at it, you know. I felt like a superhero. Man, it feels good to write a really big chunk of c code. And if you think it feels good to write it, you you would love debugging it.
cues.zh: 因为当时我做的事非常难，但问题是我很擅长，你知道吗。我感觉自己像个超级英雄。天哪，写一大段 C 代码的感觉真是太爽了。如果你觉得写代码很爽，那你调试代码的时候会更爱死那种感觉。

cues.en: But it made me feel good about myself, that was my comfort zone, you know. And then when it came time to write those reports,
cues.zh: 但这让我自我感觉良好，那可是我的舒适区，你懂的。而等到要写那些报告的时候，

cues.en: write those dashboards for doofuses,
cues.zh: 给傻瓜写那些仪表盘，

cues.en: I felt like this jerk, you know. Everybody hates SQL, right?
cues.zh: 我觉得自己像个混蛋，你知道的。大家都讨厌 SQL，对吧？

cues.en: But I was living in both worlds and a couple things started to dawn on me. The first was, you know, if you kind of squint your eyes,
cues.zh: 但我当时同时身处两个世界，有几件事慢慢让我意识到。第一件事是，你知道吗，如果你稍微眯起眼睛看，

cues.en: the work that I was doing in those two modes, it wasn't really that different. I was data wrangling. I was like giving rules about how the data was supposed to move and how it was allowed to change and so on, just in very different ways.
cues.zh: 我在那两种模式下做的工作，其实并没有那么大区别。我就是在做数据整理。我像是在规定数据该怎么流转、允许怎么变化等等，只是方式很不一样。

cues.en: And there was something kind of perverse about what the infrastructure programming I was doing in C solving those same problems over and over again, you know.
cues.zh: 而且我用 C 做基础设施编程，一遍又一遍地解决同样的问题，这其实有点反常。

cues.en: And I began to ask myself,
cues.zh: 于是我开始问自己，

cues.en: gosh. Oh, the other thing to point out is it felt good to write c, but when I wrote SQL, I wrote good programs.
cues.zh: 天哪。还有一点要指出：写 C 感觉很好，但当我写 SQL 时，我写出的是好程序。

cues.en: Like, it was easier to get the program right. It was really easy to debug. By the time I checked it in, was probably right.
cues.zh: 比如，把程序写对更容易了。调试起来真的很轻松。等我提交代码时，它大概已经是对的了。

cues.en: So I started to ask myself, gosh, like, could it be possible to use a language like SQL to write general purpose distributed systems? What what would have to what would have to change for that to be true?
cues.zh: 于是我开始问自己，天哪，有没有可能用像 SQL 这样的语言来写通用分布式系统？要实现这一点，得改变什么？

cues.en: And I can kind of explain these feels, the feeling good thing. When we write programs like c, we're interacting with computers in the way that we were trained to. Like I learned on the Texas Instruments that a program is a numbered list of instructions that tell the computer do this, do that, do this. Right? So when we think about interaction with computers, it's very natural to think of what a program does is it provides us with a mapping from the program to a set of behaviors that it induces in a system. That's where we like to be, that's where we feel comfortable.
cues.zh: 我大概能解释这些感受，也就是那种感觉很好的事。当我们写 C 这类程序时，是在用我们被训练过的方式与计算机交互。比如我在 Texas Instruments 上学到的是，程序就是一串带编号的指令，告诉计算机做这个、做那个、再做这个。对吧？所以当我们思考与计算机的交互时，很自然会认为程序做的事，就是给我们一个从程序到它在系统中引发的一组行为的映射。这正是我们喜欢待的地方，也是我们感到自在的地方。

cues.en: A language like SQL by contrast
cues.zh: 相比之下，像 SQL 这样的语言

cues.en: gives us a mapping between a program
cues.zh: 为我们提供了程序与……之间的映射

cues.en: and the outcomes it induces.
cues.zh: 以及它所引发的结果。

cues.en: Jumping over the behaviors.
cues.zh: 跳过这些行为。

cues.en: It means well,
cues.zh: 本意是好的，

cues.en: if you will, because data becomes a common language between
cues.zh: 可以这么说，因为数据成了……之间的通用语言

cues.en: the program that the programmer is laboring over and the meaning of the program. The place that the programmer's head has to go as soon as they lift up their hands from the keyboard when they start asking themselves if their program upholds the various correctness properties that they want it to. Okay? I'm arguing semantics, aren't I? I'm talking about semantics, right? So,
cues.zh: 程序员正在费力处理的程序，以及这个程序的含义。也就是程序员双手离开键盘、开始问自己程序是否满足他们想要的各种正确性属性时，脑子必须转向的地方。对吧？我是在论证语义，不是吗？我在谈语义，对吧？那么，

cues.en: you know, there's lots of different flavors of semantics, but two that I'll point out right now. Many of you may be familiar with the operational semantics of programming languages, which essentially say, a program means
cues.zh: 你知道，语义有很多种不同的流派，但这里我先指出两种。你们很多人可能都熟悉编程语言的操作语义，它基本上是说，一个程序的含义就是

cues.en: what it does to some abstract machine,
cues.zh: 它对某个抽象机器所做的事情，

cues.en: its behaviors.
cues.zh: 它的行为。

cues.en: The model theoretic semantics by contrast, semantics that are usually associated with formal logic and language theory and to a lesser degree logic programming say that, no no, the meaning of a program
